note: William Michael Griffin Jr. from Wyandanch, Long Island. With DJ Eric B., he rewrote what rapping could be in 1986–87: internal rhymes, multisyllables and a calm, low delivery when everyone else was shouting. Most MCs after him are working in his shadow.

Lawrence Parker founded Boogie Down Productions with DJ Scott La Rock, who was shot dead months after their debut, Criminal Minded (1987). He turned BDP toward 'edutainment', founded the Stop the Violence Movement, and won the Bridge Wars against MC Shan and the Juice Crew.

clips.t: MC's Act Like They Don't Know

note: Antonio Hardy, the Juice Crew's sharpest technician. Long Live the Kane (1988) set a pace — fast, articulate, effortlessly cool — that a generation studied; a young Jay-Z toured as his hype man.

Richard Walters was born in South London and moved to the Bronx at eleven. His British-inflected voice and storytelling (first heard on Doug E. Fresh's 'La Di Da Di', 1985) made The Great Adventures of Slick Rick (1988) one of the most sampled albums in rap.

Carlton Ridenhour, the baritone of Public Enemy. Over the Bomb Squad's dense noise, It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back (1988) made political rap a mass-market proposition; he called hip-hop 'Black America's CNN'.

clips.t: Black Steel in the Hour of Chaos
By the Time I Get to Arizona

aka: Kool G Rap and DJ Polo
note: Nathaniel Wilson from Corona, Queens, another Juice Crew member. His dense multis and street narratives — delivered through a slight lisp — are the template for Nas, Biggie and the whole mafioso-rap wave.

Keith Elam ('Gifted Unlimited Rhymes Universal') was the voice of Gang Starr, with DJ Premier's chopped jazz underneath. His flat, unhurried monotone is one of the most recognisable instruments in rap. He died in 2010.

Corey Penn, the rapper half of Pete Rock & CL Smooth. Mecca and the Soul Brother (1992) and 'T.R.O.Y.' — an elegy for their friend Trouble T Roy — are the high-water mark of jazz-sampling golden-era rap.
Nasir Jones from the Queensbridge Houses. His debut Illmatic (1994), made with Premier, Pete Rock, Q-Tip and Large Professor, is the reference point for New York lyricism — ten tracks, no filler.

clips.t: If I Ruled the World (Imagine That)

note: Christopher Wallace from Bedford-Stuyvesant. Ready to Die (1994) paired street detail with radio hits; his conversational flow and rich, heavy voice made him the biggest rapper in the world before his murder in March 1997, aged 24.

Shawn Carter from the Marcy Houses. He put out Reasonable Doubt (1996) on his own Roc-A-Fella label and spent the next decade as rap's dominant commercial force — writing, famously, without writing anything down.

Trevor Smith came up in Leaders of the New School and stole A Tribe Called Quest's 'Scenario' (1991). Solo, his growl and gear-changing double-time made him the loudest presence in late-'90s rap videos.

clips.t: Put Your Hands Where My Eyes Could See

note: Clifford Smith, the first Wu-Tang member to go solo with Tical (1994). Raspy, playful and impossibly relaxed, he's the Clan's most natural star.

Dennis Coles of Wu-Tang Clan. His high, urgent voice and free-associating, almost surreal detail made Ironman (1996) and Supreme Clientele (2000) cult classics; Fishscale (2006) kept the streak going.

clips.t: All That I Got Is You

note: Corey Woods of Wu-Tang Clan. Only Built 4 Cuban Linx… (1995), with Ghostface riding shotgun, invented the mafioso-rap slang and cinematic coke-trade storytelling a decade of rap borrowed.

Gary Grice, the eldest and most precise lyricist in Wu-Tang. Liquid Swords (1995), produced by his cousin RZA and laced with samurai-film dialogue, is cold, chess-like, and widely considered the best Wu solo album.
Russell Jones of Wu-Tang Clan: half-sung, half-howled, completely unpredictable. Return to the 36 Chambers: The Dirty Version (1995) is a one-off. He died in 2004, two days short of 36.
Reggie Noble, an EPMD protégé. Over funk-heavy Erick Sermon beats, Whut? Thee Album (1992) and Muddy Waters (1996) made him rap's great comic-surrealist; he and Method Man later became a double act.

clips.t: Let's Get Dirty (I Can't Get in da Club)
Let's Get Dirty (I Can't Get in da Club)

note: Dante Smith, half of Black Star with Talib Kweli. Black on Both Sides (1999) is sweeping and soulful, and he was already a working actor; he now goes by Yasiin Bey.
Talib Kweli Greene, the other half of Black Star and the conscience of the Rawkus Records era. Quality (2002), with the Kanye-produced 'Get By', was his commercial peak.
Tariq Trotter, frontman of The Roots, rap's great live band. Things Fall Apart (1999) went platinum; his wordy, rhythmic precision is easy to miss behind Questlove's drums — until you listen.
Earl Simmons. In 1998 he became the first artist to debut two albums at No. 1 in the same year. The bark, the prayers, the rough snarl: no one else sounds like DMX. He died in 2021.

Christopher Rios, a Puerto Rican MC from the Bronx and Fat Joe's Terror Squad partner. Capital Punishment (1998) was the first solo Latino rap album to go platinum; his breath control was absurd. He died in 2000, aged 28.

Daniel Dumile was Zev Love X in KMD; after his brother's death he returned in a metal mask. Operation: Doomsday (1999) and Madvillainy (2004, with Madlib) made him the underground's great wordsmith. He died in 2020.

Lonnie Rashid Lynn. 'I Used to Love H.E.R.' (1994) — hip-hop as a woman who's lost her way — sparked a feud with Ice Cube; Like Water for Chocolate (2000) and Be (2005) made him a Soulquarians fixture.
Dana Owens. All Hail the Queen (1989) and 'Ladies First' (with Monie Love) put a feminist, Afrocentric voice front and centre; 'U.N.I.T.Y.' won a Grammy in 1995, and she went on to TV and film.
Lana Moorer, who released Lyte as a Rock (1988) at 17 — the first full-length solo album by a woman rapper. Her deep, assured voice and battle record ('10% Dis') still set the bar.
Kimberly Jones, Biggie's Junior M.A.F.I.A. protégé. Hard Core (1996) was blunt, explicit and in total control of the narrative, changing what a woman in mainstream rap could say.

Marshall Mathers, discovered by Dr. Dre off a battle-rap tape. The Slim Shady LP (1999) and The Marshall Mathers LP (2000) made him the biggest-selling rapper of his era; his nasal, elastic voice can change character mid-line.
Curtis Jackson from South Jamaica, Queens, shot nine times in 2000 and dropped by Columbia. Mixtapes got him to Eminem and Dre; Get Rich or Die Tryin' (2003) sold 872,000 in its first four days.
Jason Phillips of The LOX. That gravelly voice and his signature laugh make him one of rap's most quoted guest verses; 'Why' (2004) asked the rhetorical questions.
Cameron Giles. Come Home with Me (2002) on Roc-A-Fella launched the Diplomats (Dipset); his loopy rhyme schemes and pink-mink persona became a whole aesthetic.

clips.t: What Means the World to You

note: Troy Jamerson of Organized Konfusion. 'Simon Says' (1999), built on the Godzilla theme, was his solo breakthrough — a showcase for one of the most technically intricate pens in rap.
Tracy Marrow, born in Newark, raised in LA. '6 'N the Mornin'' (1986) is often called the first gangsta-rap record; he later fronted the metal band Body Count and became a TV fixture.

clips.t: The Girl Tried to Kill Me

note: O'Shea Jackson wrote much of N.W.A's Straight Outta Compton, then left over money. AmeriKKKa's Most Wanted (1990), made in New York with the Bomb Squad, is as furious a solo debut as rap has.

clips.t: The Nigga Ya Love to Hate

note: Eric Wright co-founded Ruthless Records and N.W.A. His high, nasal voice — often reciting lyrics Ice Cube and the D.O.C. wrote — was the unlikely face of gangsta rap. He died of AIDS-related complications in 1995.
Calvin Broadus, introduced on Dr. Dre's The Chronic. Doggystyle (1993) was the first debut album to enter the Billboard 200 at No. 1; that lazy, melodic drawl is G-funk's signature.

clips.t: Ain't No Fun (If the Homies Can't Have None)

note: Tupac Shakur, born in East Harlem, started as a Digital Underground roadie and dancer. Passionate, contradictory and endlessly quotable, he was murdered in Las Vegas in September 1996, aged 25.
Todd Shaw sold tapes out of his car trunk in early-'80s Oakland. His slow, profane pimp storytelling ('Freaky Tales') built the West Coast independent model before N.W.A.

clips.t: I Want to Be Free (That's the Truth)

note: Earl Stevens, Bay Area slang inventor. Releasing through his family's Sick Wid It label, he coined or popularised phrases ('fo' shizzle', 'you feel me') the rest of rap picked up.
Alvin Joiner, part of the Likwit Crew with Tha Alkaholiks. Dr. Dre's Chronic 2001 brought him to the mainstream; later famous for MTV's Pimp My Ride.

Teren Delvon Jones, Ice Cube's cousin. He launched the Hieroglyphics crew, made the cartoonish I Wish My Brother George Was Here (1991), later fronted Deltron 3030 and rapped on Gorillaz' 'Clint Eastwood'.
Brad Jordan of the Geto Boys and Rap-A-Lot Records. Heavy, haunted storytelling about death and paranoia; peers (Jay-Z, Nas among them) routinely name him one of the greatest of all time.

clips.t: A Minute to Pray and a Second to Die

note: Christopher Bridges, an Atlanta radio DJ who signed to Def Jam South. Elastic, cartoonish voice, punchline flow; Back for the First Time (2000) and the hits that followed defined early-2000s Southern rap.
Dwayne Carter joined Cash Money at 11 and the Hot Boys at 15. Tha Carter (2004) and Tha Carter II (2005) began his transformation from teen sidekick into the most prolific rapper alive.
Terius Gray, Cash Money's breakout star. 400 Degreez (1998) and 'Back That Azz Up' took New Orleans bounce rhythms national; that sing-song drawl is pure Magnolia Projects.
Carl Mitchell was briefly listed by Guinness as the fastest rapper in the world (1992). Kamikaze (2004) made the speed commercial; Kanye produced 'Overnight Celebrity'.

Kanye West was Roc-A-Fella's in-house producer (Jay-Z's The Blueprint) before he was allowed to rap. The College Dropout (2004), recorded partly with his jaw wired shut after a car crash, changed what a mainstream rapper could look and sound like.

Jonathan Davis, later Kamaal Fareed, the Abstract of A Tribe Called Quest. His nasal, soft-spoken voice is one of hip-hop's most identifiable; Amplified (1999), co-produced with J Dilla, was his solo debut.
Kurtis Walker was the first rapper signed to a major label (Mercury, 1979). 'The Breaks' (1980) was the first certified gold 12-inch rap single.
Marcel Hall, the Juice Crew's clown prince and beatboxer. 'Just a Friend' (1989) went top 10; a sample lawsuit over his 1991 album changed how hip-hop clears samples. He died in 2021.

clips.t: This Is Something for the Radio
Make the Music with Your Mouth, Biz

note: Dwight Myers, the 'Overweight Lover' — born in Jamaica, raised in Mount Vernon. Smooth, good-humoured new jack swing rap; 'Now That We Found Love' was a worldwide hit. He died in 2011.

clips.t: The Overweight Lover's in the House

note: Melissa Elliott, writer and rapper, with Timbaland as producer. Supa Dupa Fly (1997) through Under Construction (2002) pushed rap's sound and its videos further out than anyone.
Rodney Smith from Stockwell, South London, son of a Pentecostal preacher. Run Come Save Me (2001) and 'Witness (1 Hope)' built a British rap that sounded like dub and sound systems, not New York.
Dylan Mills from Bow, East London. Boy in da Corner (2003), recorded as a teenager, won the Mercury Prize and introduced the world to grime.

Anthony Criss, lead rapper of Naughty by Nature (with Vin Rock and DJ Kay Gee), Queen Latifah protégés. 'O.P.P.' (1991) and 'Hip Hop Hooray' (1993) were crossover smashes with a hard, rapid-fire core.

Germaine Williams, born in Kingston. He picked a fight with LL Cool J in 1997 ('Second Round K.O.', with Mike Tyson in the video), and his debut Can-I-Bus (1998) was a huge hype that failed to land; a cult technical favourite ever since.
